catalog_quote: 5.2. Stress. Stress is noncontrastive on the word level; it is governed by tone and word shape. Phonetically, stress is only a greater degree of amplitude relative to unstressed syllables. In two-syllable words, each syllable is stressed equally, regardless of tone. In three-syllable words, the penultimate syllable usually takes less stress than the other two, but will take more stress if it carries the only high tone in the word. The stress can be perturbed in the context of a longer utterance, but this has not been studied in detail. ... 3.1. Inventory and Description. There are five emic tones in Tangbago: High (H) ´ Mid (M) ¯ Low (L) Falling (F) ^ Rising (R) ˇ. Falling tone glides from high pitch to low pitch. Rising tone glides from low pitch to high pitch. Low tone, when occurring utterance final, often glides from low pitch to extra low pitch.

new_statements.quote: 3.1. Inventory. There are five tones in Banda-Tangbago: High (´), Mid (¯), Low (`), Falling (^), and Rising (ˇ). An allotone of Low occurring utterance final glides from low pitch to extra low pitch. [...] 3.3. Functional load. Tone has lexical function in all word classes. In verbs and pronouns, it has grammatical function as well [...] 4.1. Configurations. There are two syllable configurations in Banda-Tangbago, V and CV. [...] Every syllable carries a tone. 4.2. Strong and weak. For the sake of convenience, CV syllables composed of a liquid and a low vowel are termed strong. Preceding CV syllables composed of a non-liquid and a simple vowel are termed weak.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda-Tangbago is described as a five-tone language (three level tones plus falling and rising) in which every syllable bears a tone and tone is lexically contrastive in all word classes and grammatically contrastive in verbs and pronouns. The description contains no statement about word stress or accent at all; its 'strong' vs 'weak' syllables are a segmental classification (liquid + low vowel vs other CV) used to state vowel-distribution restrictions, not a stress position. No word-stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: nouns usually carry only level tones (all 9 two-syllable and 27 three-syllable level-tone combinations attested); verbs lack Rising; adjectives carry level, usually identical, tones (sec. 3.2.2).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology of the Tangbago dialect recorded at Sopo, Sudan, 1982-83 (sec. 0). Sec. 8 'Intonation' describes only paragraph-level pitch register (higher onset, lower final phrase; a high register for questions/astonishment), explicitly not much contrastive intonation. Tone-mark glyphs in the quote are normalized from a garbled scanned layer; the wording is verbatim.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened primary description (Sampson 1985) covers the Tangbago dialect, studied at Sopo, South Sudan, in 1982-83. Glottolog's own coding of that reference is 'Tangbago = Banda-Ndélé [bfl]' (ref 99632) and Moñino 1988 (via Wikipedia 'Central Banda language') lists Tàngbàgò among the Bàndà-Ndele varieties, so the identity with band1345 is secure; Glottolog lists no separate dialect glottocode for Tangbago. Note that Glottolog's Cloarec-Heiss 1986 grammar attached to this languoid is coded for Banda-Bambari [liy] (Banda-Linda), not bfl.

new_statements.quote: 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué's BANDA spellings yavro (dog), yabru (goat), akblo (child) with Hackett's TOGBO renderings yavoro, aboro, agbolo. [preceded by 2a: There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages—High, Mid, and Low. Rising and Falling tones are common outside NDOGO-SERE, but seem for the most part to be the result of assimilation. Tone classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted; tone also plays a grammatical role in Verb conjugation.]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Sampson 1985 (existing statement: five-tone language; OPSL 4 sec. 5.2: stress noncontrastive, governed by tone and word shape). Tucker & Bryan add only that Banda is a level-tone language with tone classes and that stress-related penultimate shortening occurs; they give no stress placement, so nothing to contradict. Note the book describes Banda in general from Eboué (Oubangui-Chari), Tisserant 1931 and Hackett's Togbo notes; 'Tangbago', 'Linda' and 'Banda of the Sudan' have no hits in the scanned, so the remark is not specific to this languoid's Sudanese variety. Opened via archive. prior passes on 2026-09-16/17 also could not be reached by automated download), so the page…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level survey remark only: the Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi languages have three level tones (H, M, L) with lexical tone classes and grammatical tone; the 'Stress' paragraph gives no placement rule, saying only that stress affects vowel quality and length and that in Banda (as in Ngbaka and Gbaya) the penultimate syllable of trisyllables tends to be extra short (Eboué's yavro/yabru/akblo vs. Togbo yavoro/aboro/agbolo). Nothing about where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the contrast drawn is between Mayogo (penultimate lengthening) and Ngbaka/Gbaya/Banda (penultimate shortening)
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat 'BANDA' as a whole (Eboué's Oubangui-Chari Banda spellings, Tisserant's 1931 grammar, Hackett's field notes on Togbo, Mortier on Mbanja) inside a joint Sere-Mundu / Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi chapter; the Sudanese Tangbago dialect (tang1341 under band1345, described by Sampson 1985) is never named in the scanned. The catalog's existing statement (Sampson 1985) is explicitly about Tangbago of Sopo, Sudan.
